opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, because off-policy learning is both what makes something like AlphaGo practical and where a lot of the subtle failure modes come from.

On the value side, the big win is data efficiency and reuse. In an AlphaGo-style setup you have this expensive process of generating games, running MCTS, getting improved policy targets out of the search. You don't want to throw all of that away the moment your network updates by one gradient step. So you keep a replay buffer of recent self-play games and train on it, even though those games were generated by a slightly older version of the network. Strictly speaking, that's off-policy. In practice it works fine because the lag is small, and the search acts as a policy improvement operator. The MCTS visit counts are already a better target than the raw network, so you're distilling something better into the network regardless of which checkpoint produced it.

You also get the ability to bootstrap from human data. The original AlphaGo started by imitating expert games before doing self-play. That's maximally off-policy: the data comes from a totally different distribution of players. But it gets you to a competent starting point much faster than learning from random play.

The risks come from distribution mismatch. The value network is trained to predict outcomes from positions, and those outcomes depend on who was playing. If you train value estimates on games from an older or weaker policy, or from humans, the network learns "what happens from this position when *that* player continues," not what happens when your current, stronger policy continues. Then the search uses those values to guide itself, and you can get systematic errors that compound. The network is confidently wrong in exactly the parts of the state space your current policy is now steering toward, which are the parts the old data covered least.

There's a related issue with blind spots. If your training data never visits certain kinds of positions, the network has no grounding there, and an adversary can exploit that. We've seen this with the adversarial attacks on superhuman Go engines, where relatively weak agents found strategies that led the strong engine into weird positions where its value estimates just fell apart. That's at least partly a coverage problem: self-play data only covers what self-play tends to do.

So the way I think about it: off-policy data is great for getting broad coverage and amortizing compute, but you need a strong on-policy correction loop. You need fresh data from the current policy so the value function is calibrated where it matters, and ideally some mechanism like search, or a diverse league of opponents, to keep pushing into states the network hasn't seen. The danger is less "off-policy is bad" and more that you can quietly build a system whose confidence outruns its coverage.

And I think that lesson transfers pretty directly to LLMs and robotics now. Pretraining is massively off-policy, basically imitation of human data. Then RL is the on-policy correction. A lot of the open questions are really about how much you can lean on the off-policy prior versus how much fresh, self-generated experience you need to fix the places where it's miscalibrated.

r001.rationale: The response discusses distribution mismatch and states missing from training data, but does not say that supervising states the current policy would never visit wastes model capacity.

r002.rationale: It recommends fresh on-policy data and diverse opponents, but does not propose a limited share of near-optimal, off-trajectory states in a DAgger-style approach.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain that supervision on states off an optimal trajectory should teach the policy to return to that trajectory.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that AlphaGo-style systems are kind of a funny case, because the thing people remember is the self-play loop, and that part is actually on-policy in spirit. You're playing games with roughly the current policy, you're evaluating with the current value network, and the data you generate is fresh. But the original AlphaGo wasn't purely that. It bootstrapped off of a huge pile of human expert games, which is maximally off-policy. Those games were played by people with completely different priors, different search depth, different mistakes. And that off-policy data is what got the policy network to a place where MCTS could even do anything useful. If you start MCTS from a random policy on a 19 by 19 board, the search is just wandering around in the dark.

So the value of off-policy data is basically that it's a huge compute multiplier early on. You get to skip the part where you'd have to rediscover that corners and edges matter, or whatever the equivalent is in your domain. Somebody else already paid for that exploration. And I'd extend that to things like the replay buffer, which is really the same idea. You keep around trajectories from older versions of yourself, and you keep learning from them even though the current policy would never generate them anymore. That stabilizes things a lot. Pure on-policy methods can be incredibly sample inefficient and they can oscillate, where you forget a strategy and then relearn it a few iterations later.

The risk is the obvious one, which is that your value estimates are now about a distribution you're not actually in. If you train a value function on human games, it learns something like "given that a strong human got to this position, how good is it." That's a different question from "given that my policy got here, how good is it." And the distribution shift can be subtle. The classic failure is the value network gets confidently wrong in positions that humans just never play, because no human would make the move that gets you there. Then MCTS, which is a search procedure that is really good at finding exactly the states where your value function is most wrong, goes and exploits those holes. So you get this adversarial dynamic between your search and your own value estimates. AlphaGo Zero was, in part, a bet that it's cleaner to just drop the human data and eat the cost of learning from scratch, and I think the result there surprised a lot of people, including me.

There's also a more boring risk, which is that off-policy data can cap you. If you're imitating humans too hard, you inherit the human blind spots. The whole point of the system is to exceed the demonstrator, and so at some point you need a mechanism to walk away from the demonstrations. In AlphaGo that mechanism was self-play plus search, and the search is really the key ingredient, because it's a way of generating a better target than the policy itself would produce. I'd actually argue the search is doing more of the work than the off-policy versus on-policy distinction. It's a policy improvement operator that's somewhat agnostic to where the data came from.

And then when I think about this in the context of robotics, which is where I spend most of my time, the tradeoff gets much more lopsided. On-policy data is extremely expensive. Every rollout is a real robot doing real things, possibly breaking stuff. So you'd love to be off-policy. You'd love to train on teleoperation data, on data from other robots, on data from old policies. But you don't have a simulator that's as faithful as the rules of Go, so the distribution shift problems get worse, not better. There's no exact game tree to search over to correct your mistakes. So you end up in this uncomfortable middle ground where you lean on off-policy data because you have to, and then you spend a ton of effort on things like conservative value estimation or just plain old filtering, to stop the policy from going places where your estimates are garbage. I think the honest summary is that off-policy training is where most of the leverage is in practice, and the entire research problem is building the thing that lets you trust it.

r001.rationale: It describes value estimates becoming wrong on states humans never visit, but does not say that supervising on states the current policy would never visit wastes model capacity.

r002.rationale: It does not propose adding a limited share of states near but outside optimal trajectories in a DAgger-style approach.

r003.rationale: It discusses search as a way to improve targets, but does not say off-trajectory supervision should teach the policy to return to the optimal trajectory.

astra-6.text:
I think the big value is that you don’t have to rediscover everything through your own experience. In an AlphaGo-style system, you can learn from human games, from older versions of yourself, or from a search procedure that makes better decisions than your policy can make on its own. That’s a really powerful way to bootstrap learning.

The risk is that the data comes from a different distribution than the one you’ll encounter when you actually run your policy. Suppose you’re learning a value function from games played by a very strong player. A position might be winning because that player knows how to execute the next twenty moves. That doesn’t necessarily mean it’s winning for you. If you treat their outcomes as estimates of what will happen under your own behavior, you can become pretty miscalibrated.

Search helps because you can use the simulator to check your intuitions, but it also puts pressure on the value function: search can find positions that look good to the evaluator because the evaluator is wrong. So I’d think of off-policy data as a useful source of knowledge, with fresh self-play providing a correction. You want to keep testing whether the things you learned from somebody else’s experience actually translate into better decisions under your current policy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the attraction is that you can learn from experience that your current policy wouldn’t generate. In an AlphaGo-style system, search gives you a policy that’s stronger than the underlying network, and you train the network to imitate what search discovered. That’s a very powerful improvement loop: you don’t have to stumble on every good move through unaided play.

The risk is distribution shift. If you’re learning from games played by an older policy, or by a human, those games visit different positions than your current policy will visit. You can become very good at predicting what to do in that dataset without becoming equally good at playing a game, where your own decisions determine what happens next.

There’s also a distinction between learning from an actual outcome and bootstrapping from your own estimates. If you use your value function to evaluate positions, and then train on decisions that were selected because that value function liked them, you can reinforce its errors. Search helps, but finite search doesn’t automatically give you an independent ground truth.

So I’d want a loop where off-policy data gives you reuse and diversity, while fresh self-play keeps checking whether the improvements hold up under the distribution the system actually creates. The important question is whether the policy wins more games, not just whether it fits the training targets better.

r002.rationale: It proposes combining off-policy data with fresh self-play, but does not specify a limited share of states near but outside optimal trajectories or a DAgger-style approach.

r003.rationale: It does not say that supervision on off-trajectory states should teach the policy to return to an optimal trajectory.
